questions.question: A whole life policy promises a fixed death benefit whenever death occurs. The insured survives for 40 years after issue and then dies. How does this affect entitlement to the death benefit?
options: The benefit expires after the first year.
The benefit becomes payable on survival alone.
The benefit remains payable on that death.
The benefit is payable only before retirement.

questions.question: A whole life policy pays a fixed amount at death, whose time $T$ is uncertain. The interest force is fixed at $\delta>0$. Why can its present value still be random?
options: Its discount factor depends on the random death time.
Its promised amount must fluctuate with mortality.
Its interest force must change with the death time.
Its payment probability is a random discount rate.

questions.question: A unit whole life benefit is settled at the end of the death year. For continuous lifetime $T$, let $p_k=\mathbb{P}(T>k)$ at integer $k\ge0$. Which formula weights the payment at time $k+1$ in its APV for every such lifetime law?

A continuous lifetime $T$ has survival probability $S(t)>0$, density $f(t)$ and mortality force $\mu(t)=f(t)/S(t)$. A unit benefit is paid at death at interest force $\delta\ge0$. Which integrand gives its expected discounted value?
For a unit benefit paid at continuous death time $T$, let $v\in(0,1)$ be fixed and $\mathbb{E}[T]<\infty$. Which APV formula is valid for every lifetime law satisfying these conditions?

A unit whole life benefit is settled at the end of the death year. Death occurs at remaining lifetime $T=2.4$, with completed years $K=\lfloor T\rfloor$ and the annual discount factor is $v=0.9$. What is its realised present value?
A whole life benefit of 200 is paid at death. Mortality force is constant at $\lambda=0.02$ per year and interest force at $\delta=0.03$ per year. What is its actuarial present value?

A unit annual-settlement whole life benefit has discount factor $v=0.8$. Its continuous lifetime dies in the first year with probability $0.25$ and in the second with probability $0.75$. What is its actuarial present value?

A unit whole life benefit is paid at the death of a life with continuous remaining lifetime $T$ finite almost surely. Annual effective interest is zero. Which formula gives its APV for every such lifetime law?

A unit death benefit can be paid immediately at death time $T=3.6$ or at annual settlement time 4. With annual discount factor $v=0.9$, what is the annual-settlement present value divided by the immediate present value?
For an at-death unit whole life benefit with constant mortality force $\lambda>0$ and fixed interest force $\delta>0$, how does doubling $\lambda$ affect the actuarial present value?
options: It doubles the value exactly at every mortality rate.
It increases the value, but by less than a factor of two.
It decreases the value because survival becomes shorter.
It leaves the value unchanged because death remains certain.

questions.question: For an at-death unit whole life benefit, constant mortality force $\lambda>0$ is fixed. When constant interest force $\delta\ge0$ increases, what happens to its actuarial present value?
options: It increases, approaching one as $\delta$ grows.
It stays equal to the lifetime death probability one.
It decreases, approaching zero as $\delta$ grows.
It first increases and then decreases at $\delta=\lambda$.

questions.question: A unit whole life policy has continuous finite death time $T$, completed years $K=\lfloor T\rfloor$ and annual effective interest $i\ge0$. Which comparison holds between the at-death value $\bar A=\mathbb{E}[v^T]$ and annual value $A=\mathbb{E}[v^{K+1}]$, with $v=(1+i)^{-1}$?
options: $\bar A=A$ for every mortality law and interest rate.

questions.question: A continuous death time $T$ is uniform on $(0,1)$. A unit whole life benefit uses interest force $\delta=1$ per year. What are the at-death and end-of-death-year actuarial present values, in that order?

A unit whole life benefit is paid at death under constant mortality force $\lambda>0$. Its actuarial present value is $0.4$ at interest force $\delta=0.03$ per year. What mortality force is consistent with this valuation?

A life has constant mortality force $\lambda>0$. Write $r=\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda}$ for one-year survival. A unit whole life benefit is settled at the end of the death year, at discount factor $0<v<1$. What is its actuarial present value?

A unit death benefit has continuous finite death time $T$ and is valued at strictly positive interest $i$. Compare settlement at $T$ with settlement at $\lfloor T\rfloor+1$. What makes the at-death actuarial present value strictly larger?
options: The mortality force increases at every attained age.
Annual valuation discounts at the average death time.
Annual settlement delays every payment by a full year.
The settlement delay is positive with probability one.

questions.question: An assertion claims that immediate whole life settlement is always worth at least annual settlement whenever both APVs are finite. Test it with continuous death time $T$ uniform on $(0,1)$ and interest $i=-1/2$, so $v=(1+i)^{-1}=2$. What are the at-death and annual unit APVs, respectively?

A continuous remaining lifetime $T$ has survival $\mathbb{P}(T>t)=1/(1+t)$ for $t\ge0$, so $\mathbb{E}[T]=\infty$. A unit whole life benefit is paid at death at interest force $\delta=1$. What can be concluded about its actuarial present value?
options: It is finite and lies strictly between zero and one.
It is infinite because the mean lifetime is infinite.
It is zero because discounting at the mean gives zero.
It equals one because death eventually occurs surely.

questions.question: A remaining lifetime $T$ is uniform on $(0,2)$, with mortality force $\mu(t)=1/(2-t)$ for $0<t<2$. A unit benefit is paid at death at interest force $\delta=1$. What valuation correctly accounts for this varying force?
